newsitem.title: UK: Dlr/yen steadies after Hashimoto sparks stumble.
newsitem.headline: Dlr/yen steadies after Hashimoto sparks stumble.

text.p: The dollar steadied above 114 yen in early Europe after skidding more than one-yen overnight after comments by Japan's Prime Minister Ryuataro Hashimoto sent U.S. finacial markets reeling, said analysts.

Hashimoto, responding to a question after a speech at Colombia University in New York on Monday, said Japan had in the past been tempted to sell its holdings of U.S. Treasury securities and boost its gold reserves, but had not done so.
U.S. blue-chip stocks scored their second-biggest point loss, falling to 192.25 points on Monday and bond prices also fell on the comments. Dollar/yen slid to overnight lows of 114.10.

At 0735 GMT dollar/yen was at 114.35, above overnight lows, though well-down from 115.30/35 yen in late Europe on Monday. Against the mark, however, the dollar was steady to a touch firmer at 1.7241/46 against 1.7195/05 in late Europe.

"I hope the U.S. will engage in efforts and in cooperation to maintain exchange stability so we will not succumb to the temptation to sell off Treasury bills and switch our funds to gold," Hashimoto added.
In a statement released in Tokyo, the Finance Ministry said Hashimoto had been misunderstood, that the prime minister regretted his intentions had not been accurately conveyed.

"Markets were hit quite badly. We will now see a period characterised by denial and rebuttal from Japan. And by the time the U.S. opens this afternoon there should be a renewed calm and stability," said Julian Fisher, economist at Daiwa Europe.
"I wouldn't be surprised if we saw some bounce-back both in the dollar and in the treasury markets," he added.

Analysts said Hashimoto's comments reflected Japan's frustration at American warnings that Japan not let its trade surplus balloon again. U.S. President Bill Clinton warned Japan on Sunday that it risks an economic war with the U.S. if the surplus explodes again.
Markets were also surprised by Hashimoto's comments since they followed a G7 summit meeting in Denver which played down Japan's rising trade surplus, pushing dollar/yen higher.
Analysts said currency markets are now expecting Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, speaking at 1315 GMT at the Forum on the American city in Washington, to soothe the market.
Dollar/mark, however, beat to its own drum in Europe rising a touch and focusing instead on a significant softening in U.S interest-rate expectations over the past month or so, said analysts.
International Monetary Fund (IMF), however, on Tuesday said it was concerned about the rising potential for U.S. inflation and suggested interest-rate hikes might be needed soon to head it off.
"While there is little evidence of pressures on prices at present, several elements in the current situation raise concerns," said an IMF statement.
For dollar/mark, traders also noted stops placed around 1.7240/50 marks because of IMM expire on Tuesday.
